real_s1.explanation: Across these mostly dog and other furry-animal classes, the unit is weaker when the main subject faces or points left. It is stronger when the subject faces right or toward or away from the camera. The 'right over left' contrast (row 1) is the most particular to this unit: it held on new photos at the 98th percentile, while the similar units fell to 82, 24 and 0. The 'toward or away from the camera over left' contrast (row 2) also held, at the 100th percentile, but similar unit 1 is at 100 there too, so part of it is shared. Two other effects did not replicate: the preference for subjects in the middle third over the left third (row 11), and the 'no clear facing direction over left' contrast (row 3). So the effect is about which way the subject faces, not where it sits in the frame.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to furry dogs and similar long-haired mammals (terriers, spaniels, wolves, Persian cat, lesser panda, keeshond). Within those classes, its clearest replicated feature is weaker activity when the main subject faces or points left. Right-facing and camera-facing subjects drive it about equally. This looks like suppression of left-facing subjects rather than a preference for one direction. The left-third position effect and the no-clear-direction comparison did not replicate. Size, framing, tint and background effects are mild and mostly shared with similar units.

real_s3.explanation: Within its top classes (furry, long-haired dogs and similar mammals such as terriers, spaniels, wolves, the Persian cat and the lesser panda), the unit is less active when the main subject faces or points left. It is about equally active for subjects facing right or facing toward or away from the camera, and both of those contrasts with left-facing held on new photos. The comparison of 'no clear direction' against left did not reach the 95th percentile on new photos, so it is less certain. Similar units partly share the toward-camera-vs-left effect, but the right-vs-left effect is more particular to this unit on new photos. A weaker dip for subjects in the left third of the frame (row 11) fits the same left-side pattern, but it is largely shared with the similar units and was not tested.

null_s1.explanation: On top dog and furry-animal classes, the unit looked weaker when the main subject faced left or sat in the left third of the frame (rows 1, 2, 3, 11). This leftward bias did not replicate on new photos. Row 1 kept its direction but fell to the 84th percentile, and rows 2, 3 and 11 dropped to about the 55th. The similar units were often as high or higher, so any mild left/right preference is shared across this group of units rather than specific to this one. The untested rows were all modest (mostly below the 90th percentile) or also shared with the similar units: subject size, cropping, warm tint and absence of straight lines. No attribute in the table reliably and specifically describes this unit beyond its class preferences.

null_s2.explanation: The unit is most active on photos of furry, long-haired dogs and similar mammals (terriers, spaniels, wolves, Saint Bernard, Persian cat, lesser panda, meerkat). Within those classes, none of the questioned photo properties reliably sets it apart. The apparent weaker response to left-facing or left-placed subjects did not replicate on new photos: right vs left dropped to the 84th percentile and the others to about the 55th. The remaining effects (larger, cut-off, warm-tinted subjects, no straight lines) are modest and largely shared with similar units, so the unit is best described by its preferred classes rather than by any particular pose or framing.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on furry mammals, mostly long-haired dog breeds plus wolves, Persian cat, lesser panda, meerkat and guenon. Within these classes, no photo property clearly and specifically drives it. The apparent dip for left-facing subjects (rows 1-3) weakened to ordinary percentiles (56-84) on new photos, so it does not reliably describe this unit. The remaining tendencies are a weaker response when the subject sits in the left third (row 11), when it is small or fully inside the frame, and when the photo has a cool tint. These are modest, and most are shared with the similar units rather than particular to this one. There is not enough evidence to say confidently that any row describes this unit specifically.
